posts.quote: THE SUBSTITUTE NEVER KNEW OUR NAMES, SO WE TRADED SEATS ALL DAY AND SHE NEVER NOTICED.
posts.caption: The note on the board said Mrs. Hadley was out, and a whisper went down the rows before the substitute even found the chalk. She carried a seating chart, which was the first mistake. By the time she finished the roll call, three of us had quietly moved two desks over. The tall boy sat in the front row as the girl with the braids, and she answered to his name without blinking. All day the poor woman called on the wrong person, and the wrong person always knew the answer. We felt like the cleverest class in the building until Mrs. Hadley came back on Thursday and read the sub's report out loud.
posts.first: I once got a whole spelling test marked under another boy's name, and he got the grade I earned. We called it even years later. Some things you only ever confess at a reunion.

posts.quote: THE LAUNDROMAT BULLETIN BOARD WAS HOW THE WHOLE TOWN FOUND A USED CRIB.
posts.caption: Every laundromat had a corkboard by the door, and it was crowded with index cards held down by pushpins. A cord of wood for sale, a crib that was barely used, piano lessons, a lost beagle with a name and a phone number. You read every card while the dryers tumbled, because you had thirty minutes and nothing else to do. The little strips along the bottom were torn off one at a time, and you could tell a card was popular when the strips ran out.
posts.first: We found our first dresser through a card on a board just like that one. The woman wanted twelve dollars and threw in the drawer pulls. Dad carried it up three flights of stairs on his back.

posts.quote: The best seat in church was the back pew by the door, and every family had one it never gave up.
posts.first: Our family had the third pew on the left, and I couldn't tell you why. Nobody ever assigned it. It was just where we sat for twenty years.

posts.quote: SLIDE NIGHT / A PROJECTOR, A BEDSHEET, AND EVERY VACATION IN ORDER
posts.caption: Somebody pinned a white bedsheet to the living room curtain rod, and everyone knew what the evening held. Dad threaded the round tray into the projector, and the fan started up with a hum. The first slide always went in upside down, and the room groaned on cue. Then came the lake cabin, the Grand Canyon, and thirty pictures of the same motel pool. The projector clicked forward and every picture glowed bigger than life on the wall. Dad narrated each one as if it had been a great expedition, and nobody dared to leave before the last slide.
posts.first: My father numbered every slide tray in pencil on the lid. He kept them in a shoebox on the closet shelf until he passed. I have the box now, and I still can't make myself throw a single one out.

posts.quote: THE FIRE DEPARTMENT FLOODED THE BALLFIELD EVERY DECEMBER, AND THAT WAS OUR ICE RINK.
posts.caption: The trucks came out the first week the ground froze hard. The firemen unrolled the canvas hose across the outfield and let it run until the water spread out flat. By the next morning the whole ballfield was a gray sheet of ice with a snowbank for a border. Kids showed up with hand-me-down skates two sizes too big, laced up with an extra pair of socks. Somebody always brought a coffee can of hot chocolate and a stack of paper cups. The ice was bumpy and the hockey pucks were old rubber balls, and we skated until the streetlights buzzed on.
posts.first: My skates came from my cousin and the left one had a different color lace. I fell more than I skated that first winter. One of the firemen used to stand at the edge in his big coat and make sure the little ones got up again.

posts.character: Values and community (the roadside fruit stand)
posts.quote: THE FRUIT STAND HAD A COFFEE CAN FOR THE MONEY AND NOBODY WATCHING IT.
posts.caption: You'd see the hand-lettered sign from a quarter mile off. Peaches this week, corn next, and a plywood table in the shade of a maple. Prices were chalked on a slate, a dollar a basket, and a coffee can sat on the end with a slot cut in the plastic lid. Whoever ran the farm was out in the field and never came to the road. You took what you wanted, dropped your money in the can, and drove on with the windows down. It never occurred to anyone to do it differently.
posts.first: We stopped at one on the way to my grandmother's every August. My father always left a little extra and said the corn was worth it. I don't think he ever met the man who grew it.

posts.quote: BALING HAY WAS A TEENAGE JOB, AND THE PAY WAS A DOLLAR AN HOUR AND ALL THE WATER YOU COULD DRINK.
posts.caption: The farmer picked you up at six in the morning in a truck with no door on the passenger side. By nine the hay was already in your collar and down your shirt. Each bale weighed about what you did, and the stack on the wagon grew higher with every row. At noon his wife sent out a jug of cold water with a dishrag wrapped around it, and it tasted better than anything you'd ever had. You went home itching and sunburned with a few dollars folded in your pocket. You slept like a stone, and you went back the next day.
posts.first: I baled hay for two summers for a man named Mr. Voss. He never raised his voice once, and he never let anyone quit early. I learned more about showing up from him than from anyone at school.

posts.quote: Every neighborhood had one house with the good yard for kickball, and its owner just accepted it.
posts.first: The Hendersons had the flat yard with the maple for second base. Mrs. Henderson never once complained about the bare patches. She just kept a pitcher of lemonade on the porch step.

posts.quote: THE COUNTY FAIR / A BLUE RIBBON, A TENT FULL OF QUILTS, AND PIES IN A ROW
posts.caption: The home arts tent was the first stop for half the women in town. Quilts hung on clotheslines strung from pole to pole, and the judges walked the aisles with clipboards. Jars of pickles and jam sat in rows with little paper tags, each one waiting on a ribbon. Pie tables were a different matter altogether, with a rivalry going back thirty years. The blue ribbon went home pinned to the kitchen wall and stayed there until the next August. You could tell who'd won by how straight she stood on the walk to the car.
posts.first: My grandmother won a red ribbon for her rhubarb pie eleven years in a row. She always said red was fine because blue got you talked about. She kept every one in the same drawer as the good tablecloth.

posts.character: Cars and driving culture (the glove box)
posts.quote: THE GLOVE BOX HELD A ROAD MAP, A TIRE GAUGE, AND EVERY RECEIPT DAD HAD EVER KEPT.
posts.caption: Nobody was allowed to open the glove box unless Dad said so. When he finally did, the door dropped down on its little hinge and out slid a folded map that would never fold the same way again. Underneath were a tire gauge, a flashlight with weak batteries, a pencil stub, and a stack of gas receipts held by a rubber band. He could tell you what he paid for fuel in 1964 and which station charged it. We kids were convinced there was a secret compartment behind it all. There wasn't, but we looked every time.
posts.first: Dad's glove box smelled like old paper and peppermint. He kept a single butterscotch candy in there for the long drives and gave it to whoever hadn't complained. It was usually my sister.
